messages:
Maya: Heads up — we're seeing apiserver 503 spikes in eu-west1 tied to GPU provisioning flows. Watch-cache queue depth is off the charts and attach ops are spiking. https://grafana.redwood/api/d/abcd1234

Sahil: looking now. watch_cache_queue ~120k, apiserver p95 ~420ms, sustained for ~6m. Lots of kv write bursts during compact window.

infra-bot: alert: watchcache_lag_seconds > 30s (eu-west1 cluster)

Owen: Did we change the provisioner batcher recently? We rolled the multi-attach batching change last night. Could be a producer burst to control plane.

Carla: yeah we flipped the large-batch feature to improve attach throughput for bulk onboarding. It reduces GPU attach time overall but bursts a ton of controller reconcilers at once.

Lee (oncall): If the controller-manager is pushing too many watch updates into apiserver at once, watch-cache eviction will thrash. Short term: we can disable large-batch path and limit attach concurrency.

Maya: sharing a quick sample of the apiserver logs around the spike:
```
I0304 12:34:56.789 main.go:123] Serving securely on 0.0.0.0:6443
E0304 12:35:02.012 watcher.go:87] watch cache backlog exceeded threshold, queue_depth=121234
E0304 12:35:02.045 proxy.go:214] 503 GET /api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/pods (10.10.2.3): upstream timeout
```

Sahil: quick mitigation plan: 1) scale apiserver replicas +10% 2) throttle provisioner attach concurrency `--max-attach-parallel=6` 3) flip large-batch feature flag off in provisioner. That buys headroom while we debug compaction timing.

Owen: also want to verify networking — saw retry counts and retransmits on nat-gw earlier which amplify latency when the controlplane is busy. `tc -s qdisc` shows a spike in dropped packets on the gw. If MTU mismatch exists between nat and host, that can increase packet fragmentation and etch into RTT.

Carla: cost tradeoff note: small batches will increase per-attach overhead; our rough calc is ~12% higher attach cost at current rates, but it prevents large-scale restarts and SLA breaches. I vote to accept short-term cost increase.

Lee (oncall): I'm going to apply the throttle and disable the large-batch flag now. Will scale apiserver after that if latency doesn't drop. @Maya please monitor dashboards.

Lee (oncall): command I'm applying:
```bash
kubectl -n infra set env deployment/provisioner PROVISIONER_MAX_ATTACH_PARALLEL=6 
kubectl -n infra patch deployment/provisioner -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"feature.largeBatch":"false"}}}}}'
```

infra-bot: action: rollout started deployment/provisioner (infra) by Lee (oncall)

Lee (oncall): patch applied, rollout in progress (10 replicas).

infra-bot: metric update: watchcache_lag_seconds -> 7s (down from 32s)

Sahil: p95 apiserver latency down to 120ms after the change, attach errors dropped. Looks promising.

Maya: confirming. I'll keep the scaling plan as a standby and revert the large-batch flag only after a 30m steady state.

Carla: raising a follow-up PR with a queue-aware batching strategy (rate-limited producer) and a cost analysis. We should avoid flip/flop by adding automated throttling based on watchcache depth.

Owen: also adding a small observability patch to emit provisioner attach burst metrics to the control plane dashboard.

Maya: Thanks all. Recording post-incident TODOs: (1) queue-aware batching PR (Carla), (2) nat-gw MTU check + fix if needed (Owen), (3) add automated throttle tied to watchcache depth (Sahil), (4) review compact schedule to avoid overlap with heavy onboarding windows.

Lee (oncall): I'll keep an eye on retries for the next hour, ping me if any regression.

Maya: Closing thread if things stay stable for 30m. :thumbsup:
